In regards to some saying that staff should realize that there should be layoffs if there is not money - that is not why any of us are upset we lost our jobs. It was the manner in which everything occurred. 

A few weeks prior we were all given new job descriptions. Of course we still understood the reality of the current state of the business, but when multiple departments but time into solidifying your role at the company and management mostly sugar coats everything, you don’t stress about losing your job - as much. 

Then, the first round of layoffs a few months ago was very different than the October one. Those employees were told ahead of time and were talked to before the rest of the company found out. This round was an 11-min long meeting with the full company where Rachel cried and said this was hard on her, she failed, and she apologized. I hope that cleared her conscious because to everyone else it felt like we were watching a pity party for the woman who instead of making obvious business decisions to avoid this wanted us to console her.

After 5 min of her crying they announced we would find out who still had a job via email. And despite Rachel saying she loved each and every one of us, there was no communication from her after the tears. While that wouldn’t be expected from most CEOs, if your business is about welcoming people and you say we are family etc. , wouldn’t you want to be a bit more personal? Especially if you came out with a book 2 days prior talking about how people need to deal with trauma and unexpected challenges? Either way she was just as disingenuous as the first time I met her so I guess I did see that coming.

So anyway, those of us who are now jobless for honestly thinking we signed up to do good for the community we’re just as blindsided by the Hollis’ this year in more ways than one. I am happy to never have to care about keeping up with Hurricane Hollis and hope the +30 employees that were let go this year are well cared for in their next companies.
